steps.title: Golden Rule
steps.body: Every piece of writing should be shaped by who will read it (audience) and what you want to achieve (purpose). These two factors determine your tone, vocabulary, structure, and style.

steps.title: Key idea 2
steps.body: What age group are they? What do they already know about the topic? What is their likely attitude toward the subject? What tone will engage them? What vocabulary level is appropriate?

steps.title: Top Tip
steps.body: The exam usually requires a formal or semi-formal tone. However, you must still adapt your writing to the specific audience - a speech to teenagers will be different from a letter to an MP, even if both are formal.

steps.title: Consider
steps.body: Age appropriateness - younger audiences need simpler vocabulary Subject knowledge - experts understand technical terms Cultural awareness - references must be accessible Tone requirements - emotive words for persuasion, neutral for information

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: How would your writing differ if addressing a headteacher versus addressing your peers? | Explain the difference between writing to persuade and writing to inform. | A speech about healthy eating - how would tone differ for primary school children versus adults?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Headteacher: formal register, respectful tone, evidence-based arguments, no contractions. Peers: informal register, relatable tone, personal examples, contractions acceptable. | Persuade aims to convince the reader to agree or take action, using rhetorical devices and emotional appeal. Inform aims to provide facts objectively, with neutral language and clear explanations. | Primary children: simple vocabulary, fun analogies, engaging tone, direct address like "your body needs..." Adults: more sophisticated vocabulary, statistics and evidence, respectful tone, addressing

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Circle or highlight the audience and purpose in the question Plan your tone and style before writing Match your vocabulary to your audience's knowledge level Keep your purpose in mind throughout - every paragraph should serve it Maintain consistent register - don't switch between formal and informal Use direct address for speeches and articles to connect with audience Check that your tone matches what the question asks for
